explain.say: The first Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State opened in July 1940. Its deck was unusually slim and flexible, and it bounced so much in wind that people nicknamed it Galloping Gertie.

explain.say: This was flutter: as the deck twisted, the wind pushed harder on it, feeding more energy into each twist. It was not simply gusts matching a rhythm; the steady wind and the deck's motion fed each other.

faq.q: Why did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse?
faq.a: Its deck was very slender and flexible. In November 1940 a steady wind set it twisting, and the twisting made the wind push harder, a feedback called flutter, until the deck tore apart.

faq.q: Why was the Tacoma Narrows deck so flexible?
faq.a: To save money, it used shallow solid girders instead of a deep, open truss, making the deck thin, narrow and very easy to bend and twist for its length.
asks: What was wrong with the Tacoma bridge design?

faq.a: Flutter is when a structure's movement in the wind changes the wind forces on it so they push it even further, feeding more energy in with each cycle. The motion grows until something breaks.
asks: Was Tacoma Narrows caused by resonance?

faq.q: How do engineers stop bridges twisting in wind?
faq.a: They test models in wind tunnels, make decks stiff against twisting, and shape them like streamlined boxes or open trusses so air flows past smoothly.
asks: How are bridges made safe in wind?

faq.q: Was anyone hurt when the Tacoma bridge fell?
faq.a: No people died. The bridge had been closed as it twisted, but a dog left in a car on the deck was lost. The collapse was filmed, and the footage is still used to teach engineers.
asks: Did anyone die in the Tacoma Narrows collapse?

facts: The first Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened on 1 July 1940 and collapsed on 7 November 1940 in a wind of about 65 kilometres per hour.
After Tacoma Narrows, wind tunnel testing of long-span bridge designs became standard practice.
